entry.title: Watch Bill Hader Explain the Many Influences That Led to His First Film, ‘They Know’
entry.summary: Bill Hader revealed details about his upcoming horror film "They Know" with Linda Cardellini — and what nobody tells filmmakers about making a debut.
entry.content:
Bill Hader has always wanted to direct a feature film. It’s just taken him a while to get to it.

“That was the dream forever. I just took the most circuitous way to get there,” Hader said. Then he cracked, “I think Kurosawa did that? Didn’t he go to a sketch comedy show for eight years? Wasn’t he in ‘Trainwreck’?”

After a long tenure on “Saturday Night Live,” starring roles in several films and co-creating his own Emmy-winning HBO series “Barry,” Hader finally got around to directing his own movie, “They Know.” In a one-on-one conversation called “What No One Tells You About Directing Your First Feature,” Hader unpacked exactly that for the audience at IndieWire‘s Future of Filmmaking 2026 Summit presented by AT&T in Los Angeles on Saturday.

Related Stories
Will ‘Wicker’ Be Black Bear’s First Big Breakout?
Pawel Pawlikowski’s Historical Stunner ‘Fatherland’ Is About Far More Than Thomas Mann — It’s About Today’s Own Fissures

With “They Know,” Hader is the latest major comedic talent to make the jump to the horror genre. As he did on “Barry,” Hader writes, directs and acts in the feature. He stars as a divorced father who begins to suspect that his ex-wife’s secret new partner is having an unorthodox effect on his children. The MRC-produced film, which also stars Linda Cardellini, wrapped photography in May and is currently in the sound-mixing stage and prepping to show to distributors.

Hader shared that the premise for the film came about from personal conversations he had with his longtime collaborator and writing partner, Duffy Boudreau.

“We’re both divorced. We were talking about how lucky we were that we were on, like, we had really good terms with our ex-wives, and we have kids with them,” Hader told Chris O’Falt, IndieWire’s VP of features strategy and host of the Filmmaker Toolkit podcast. “We started talking about the worst case scenarios of, ‘Oh, my god, this person is going through this and this person is going through that.’ And then this idea came up.”

While keeping the plot details vague, Hader admitted that he “kind of gave up on” the film for a while, as the ending of each draft felt “like every other horror movie.” But a curious new release in 2025, about the unsavory world of online scalpers, finally tipped him back towards the project.

“I went to the Nuart [Theater] by myself and I saw the movie ‘Cloud,’ by Kiyoshi Kurosawa,” he said. “And, [my movie] is nothing like that movie. But, for some reason, I saw that movie and I walked out and I was like, ‘I think I know how to do it.’ You would never see this movie and think ‘Cloud,’ but that’s where it’s at.”

A feature project has been long in the works for Hader, one of the most conspicuous cinephiles to emerge from the cast of “SNL.” (Check his second visit to the Criterion Closet, in which he pulls a whopping 15 titles — including Robert Bresson’s “A Man Escaped,” “Salvatore Giuliano” and an Allan King box set.) After helming many episodes of “Barry” — and earning a Directors Guild of America award in 2019 for the series — a push into feature filmmaking has seemed inevitable for several years.

Nonetheless, Hader maintains that he was carrying some self-doubt heading into the project, something he’s had since his sketch comedy days.

“‘SNL’ helped with that. You would just get shot down constantly. It was horrible,” Hader said with a smile. “But, in doing that, you are working on instinct.”

That healthy amount of fear helped Hader foster collaborative conversations throughout the filmmaking process, whether it was testing the looks of different lenses on location scouts or talking through his shot lists with his editor in pre-production.

“The doubt is always there. And that’s good though. If you’re not scared, then you’re fucked,” Hader said. “I met someone who worked with [Martin] Scorsese. He said the best thing about it was that he would start a day and go, ‘I don’t know what I’m doing. I don’t know what this is.’ And that’s just freeing. … We’re all scared. The worst is when people come in like, ‘I know what’s going on.’ And within five minutes you’re like, ‘The director doesn’t know what they’re doing.'”

Hader returned to the sentiment in the home-stretch of the conversation, underlining the takeaway to the crowd.

“Don’t be afraid to be wrong. That’s the thing that screwed me up. I was so terrified of looking like an idiot,” he said. “Be wrong as fast as you can be. Like, this is all wrong, but it doesn’t matter. We’re just going to. We’re going to be OK. Just keep moving.”

Along with Hader’s “What No One Tells You About Directing Your First Feature” presentation, IndieWire’s Future of Filmmaking Summit also included a keynote by directors Phil Lord and Chris Miller, diving into the production of their sci-fi blockbuster “Project Hail Mary,” and an appearance by “Obsession” writer/director Curry Barker, who was presented with IndieWire’s inaugural Future of Filmmaking award.

Watch the complete conversation with Hader in the video above.

IndieWire Future of Filmmaking 2026 Summit is presented by AT&T Untold Stories, an impactful multi-year collaboration between AT&T and Tribeca Festival that awards $1.2 million dollars, mentorship, and comprehensive support to the next generation of filmmakers looking to bring their films to the big screen. For more information, visit here.

entry.title: ‘Yaga’ Review: Hudson Williams’ Creepy Dual Roles Can’t Save a Witchy Mystery That’s Not Creepy Enough
entry.summary: A reimagining of the Baba Yaga myth (and her own play), Kat Sandler's AMC+ series follows a beat cop and a private investigator.
entry.content:
When the name Baba Yaga is first thrown out in Kat Sandler’s series, “Yaga,” the reaction is what you’d expect from any thirty-something guy in the year 2026: “Wait, the one from ‘John Wick’?” The response doubles as an acknowledgement of and explanation for a title that, on its own, sounds weirdly incomplete: “Oh, OK: They couldn’t call it ‘Baba Yaga’ because then everyone would think it’s a ‘John Wick’ show. So it’s just called, ‘Yaga.’ Because it’s actually about witches.”

But “Yaga” is also weirdly incomplete in execution, mainly because it’s not nearly weird enough. Adapted from Sandler’s play of the same name, the eight-episode series reimagines the Baba Yaga myth as a detective-driven mystery — not the myth about Keanu Reeves’ unkillable assassin, but the historical one from Slavic folklore about a witch who, depending on the teller, is either a nice, accommodating, elderly woman, or a kidnapping, kid-eating monster.

Related Stories
‘The Only Living Pickpocket in New York’ Review: An Old School Thief Holds on in the Age of Apple Pay
‘Wicker’ Review: Olivia Colman Rides Alexander Skarsgård’s Wood in Bawdy Sex Fantasy About Hysterically Horny Villagers

Sandler’s story savors teasing both potential interpretations, presenting its witchy characters as simultaneously suspicious and helpful to make sure either explanation remains plausible as long as possible: They’re there to prey on the townsfolk, or they’re there to help our investigators crack the case. Or, perhaps, it’s a little bit of both.

But “Yaga” never reaches its potential as a horror show or a mystery (and I can’t say whether its feminist underpinnings pay off either, since only seven of the eight episodes were made available for review). It’s not scary enough to qualify as the former or bewitching enough to sustain the latter. Instead, it leans on traditional, less exciting crime drama tropes while stretching out a whodunit that spends way too long pretending the answer won’t involve double, double toil and trouble, burning fire and cauldron bubbles. As fun as it is to watch Carrie-Anne Moss toy with various fuckboys, it would be nice to know why she’s doing it much, much sooner (if at all).

Things pop off with the disappearance of Henry Park (played by “Heated Rivalry’s” Hudson Williams in yet another Crave production). Henry is the heir to his family fishing empire, but he’s better known around their small, coastal town as a bro who throws great parties. He lives in a giant mansion with one (1) roommate: a friend named Logan who, despite being unrelated, looks exactly like Henry. Both roles are played by Williams, and while neither takes up that much screentime, the actor does a fine job distinguishing the entitled playboy from his quiet, fawning sidekick.

Our leads, of course, are our detectives: There’s Carson (Clark Backo), a by-the-book beat cop in the Whittock police department whose personal life is vastly underdeveloped, and Rapp (Noah Reid), a private investigator flown in (literally) by the Park family who sucks up too much oxygen. When Rapp gets dropped off at Henry’s house by helicopter, Carson takes one look at his outfit and laughs: black skinny tie, black leather jacket, brown leather duffel bag. He’s not dressed for the rainy Canadian countryside, but another cop says exactly what Rapp hopes he’ll say: “I think he looks pretty cool.”

Rapp’s first impression proves right on the nose: He’s impossibly full of himself. Cocksure and brazen, Rapp is paired with Carson by the local chief, but he doesn’t work well with others. He chases his own theories while searching for Henry (which conveniently involve a lot of drug-fueled parties and women amenable to his charms) and follows up however he feels like it (or if he feels like it, in case he’s moved on to another amenable woman). If that means a little unlawful search and seizure, so be it. If it means sleeping with a suspect (or two, or three), well that’s just a perk of the job.

Rapp comes off as such a clichéd bad boy you can’t wait for Carson to pop his inflated ego, and “Yaga” acknowledges that desire almost as quickly as it establishes the need for it. When Rapp climbs out of the helicopter to introduce himself, smoothing his hair back into place after the whirling blades displace his slick, faux-casual styling, he slips and eats dirt. Great! Get him, “Yaga!” This guy sucks, and he could only be coded as more of a douchebag if he was hocking crypto on the side and smoking cigarettes for the health benefits.

But then…he just… sticks around? Unchecked and encouraged for reasons yet unknown? Rapp’s schtick goes on for so long, working his “magic” on so many Whittock women, I found myself wondering, “Is Noah Reid Canada’s version of Ryan Gosling?” No, of course not! Ryan Gosling is Canada’s version of Ryan Gosling! Plus, if anyone in the “Yaga” cast should be treated like the most irresistible man in the northernmost part of North America, it’s Hudson Williams. After “Heated Rivalry,” no one would think twice about that guy going to bed with anyone he wants, even if he also had the worst game in town.

“Yaga” does offer some delicious comeuppance in the form of seductive, empowered suspects like Katherine (Carrie-Anne Moss), a professor who loves bones so much she wrote a book called — I am not kidding — ”Sexy Bones.” And there are a few sexy scenes here and there, although they’re usually creep-ified by ominous narration from a yet-unseen witch, disturbing hallucinations, or Rapp’s involvement.

“Yaga” feels like it’s building to a welcome point — about society’s centuries-long persecution and distrust of women, about the appropriate response to condoned oppression, about bad men with good hair — but the subtext isn’t enough to sustain eight episodes, even when they clock in at roughly 30 minutes apiece. It doesn’t help that our de facto protagonist, Carson, is a complete blank. If she was able or willing to balance out Rapp’s toxic energy, maybe “Yaga” could cast a convincing spell. As is, it’s a lot of incantations without the ensuing enchantment.

Grade: C

“Yaga” premieres Friday, October 23 on AMC+ with two episodes. New episodes will be released weekly through the two-episode finale on Friday, November 27.

entry.title: Will ‘Wicker’ Be Black Bear’s First Big Breakout?
entry.summary: With 'Wicker,' an off-beat, erotic drama, will Black Bear's have a breakout box office hit?
entry.content:
Black Bear CEO Teddy Schwarzman has seen some ups and downs in the transition from financier-producer-foreign-sales-company-UK-distributor to full-on North American distribution company Black Bear Pictures. The Blackstone scion is smart and experienced enough to know the risks inherent in competing in the fraught indie marketplace. But even in the face of frosty reviews for “Christy,” starring Sydney Sweeney with her bosom buried from view in a boxing movie, he mounted a full-on theatrical release and demonstrated his support for the filmmakers and would-be Oscar contender.

That didn’t happen. The $15-million movie grossed just under $2 million domestic. A year later, Schwarzman is soldiering on, having rejiggered his 65-person staff and executive team (CAA import Ben Kramer left earlier this year) and betting on a range of indie films from critics’ faves “The Rivals of Amziah King” (which died at the box office) and “Tuner” ($14.6 million worldwide) to the Jason Statham survival adventure “Shelter” ($56 million worldwide), Jake Gyllenhaal action thriller “In the Grey” ($28.4 million worldwide) and “Spa Weekend” ($13.9 million worldwide).

Related Stories
Pawel Pawlikowski’s Historical Stunner ‘Fatherland’ Is About Far More Than Thomas Mann — It’s About Today’s Own Fissures
‘The Only Living Pickpocket in New York’ Review: An Old School Thief Holds on in the Age of Apple Pay

This weekend Black Bear is releasing Sundance breakout “Wicker” in 1,400 theaters, where it is expected to open to $6 to $8 million. The medieval-period romance showcases British star Olivia Colman as a spinster fishmonger who commissions a wicker husband (Alexander Skarsgard). He wildly exceeds her romantic fantasies, breaks her bed, and upends every marriage in the village.

Black Bear joined the project at the script stage as international sales agent, partnering with financiers Topic and Tango. When Black Bear finally saw how the film played at Sundance, they acquired North American distribution rights. “What we’ve always tried to do with Black Bear,” said Schwarzman on Zoom, “is find films that are original, or stand out in their genre, have a real vision from a director standpoint, and make you feel in some way. … We couldn’t find a more original film than ‘Wicker,’ despite the fact that it’s an adapted short story, but the entire conceit was executed near perfection. … We were blown away that there was something weird and provocative and horny and sexual and ultimately actually incredibly emotional and human.”

Black Bear has also hired a new marketing team, scooping up former Neon executive Bianca Parkes, a graphics whiz who knows strategy, guerilla marketing, print campaigns, and merchandising, after her husband Christian left to found Clockwork at Warner Bros., as well as PR vet Heather Phillips, who has worked all sides of the studio/indie street. The “Wicker” marketing has been inspired, from a 6 foot 6 wicker standee to the “dream boyfriend” campaign.

Leaning into the weird side of this romantic fantasy, the “Wicker” trailer went viral across Black Bear’s owned channels, generating 80.3 million views in its first two weeks, with 70.5 million of those views coming organically (nearly 88 percent), generating social media conversations far and wide. On TikTok alone, trailer-related reactions and user-generated content amassed an additional 322 million views, bringing the combined total to over 402 million views. Needless to say, this evidence of consumer interest boosted the distributor’s confidence in the film’s commerciality.

The rap on Black Bear, which they deny, is that they don’t spend. Schwarzman is considered to be frugal. But they are spending now. They learned from watching Netflix’s handling of another Sundance hit, “Train Dreams,” which relaunched with a fresh campaign at the fall festivals with strong results.

Thus “Wicker” played a selection of fall festivals, skipping Toronto but selling out instantly at Middleburg. On the awards front “The Favourite” Oscar-winner Colman (boasting new hair extensions imitated on the red carpet by the ingenious Skarsgard) is in the Actress conversation as well as the hair and makeup team.

Schwarzman has figured out his ongoing strategy, he said, “We are now having a true north of the type of movies that we want to be making and that we want to be releasing, which are filmmaker-centric, original, entertaining, and with some substance to what they are.”

In today’s trying times, it may be that a sexy escapist fantasy is just what audiences need.

entry.title: Pawel Pawlikowski’s Historical Stunner ‘Fatherland’ Is About Far More Than Thomas Mann — It’s About Today’s Own Fissures
entry.summary: The filmmaker tells IndieWire about finding resonant conflicts in his moving post-war Cannes hit that completes his black-and-white period trilogy.
entry.content:
[Editor’s note: This interview was originally published during the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. MUBI opens “Fatherland” in select theaters starting Friday, October 23.]

Pawel Pawlikowski‘s seventh feature “Fatherland” came into the Cannes Competition with high expectations, and judging from audience and critical reaction, it should win a prize or two. Sandra Hüller is a frontrunner for Best Actress, having just won that award in Berlin for “Rose.” After all, this is the Polish filmmaker behind Oscar nominee “Cold War” (2018) and Oscar winner “Ida” (2013).

And, given that “Fatherland” also parses European history through complicated characters, and is filmed in black-and-white in the Academy ratio, Pawlikowski grants that he has unintentionally fashioned a trilogy.

Related Stories
‘The Only Living Pickpocket in New York’ Review: An Old School Thief Holds on in the Age of Apple Pay
Daniel Pemberton on Scoring ‘Without a Map,’ from ‘Project Hail Mary’ to David Byrne and Elon Musk

The movie confronts Germany’s post-World War II trauma in a family road movie centered on three characters: the Nobel Laureate novelist Thomas Mann (Hanns Zischler), his daughter and assistant Erika (Hüller), and his son Klaus (August Diehl). The movie kicks off with a bravura five-and-a-half minute locked-off single take of Klaus in Cannes, sitting naked on the floor by a bed with a sleeping young man. He talks on the phone with Erika, who tries to coax her depressed drug-addict intellectual twin to come on a road trip with her back to Germany as his father accepts the Goethe prize.

“When is the last time you felt anything?,” he asks.

I sat down with Pawlikowski at the J.W. Marriott in Cannes. The father-daughter relationship at the center of this heady literary movie about the “collapse of Europe,” he said, “seems to connect things.” While Italian producers initially pitched him the Colm Tóibín fictional biography of Thomas Mann, the filmmaker rejected making a biopic. But something in the book triggered the nugget of what would become “Fatherland.”

“There is this little moment, which I use as a starting point to invent a story,” he said. “When Thomas goes to Germany, he’s in an interesting situation. It rang a bell. Everything’s collapsed, everything he believed in. He’s trying to regenerate it in a one-man operation. He tries to bring together Germany and transcend the ideological division.”

Scenes of the humanist Mann speaking earnestly to auditoriums full of people who likely do not hear him are strangely resonant with today. (Pawlikowski put enormous time into finding the right faces for the extras.) “He’s like a boxer going into the ring,” said Pawlikowski. “That’s his big entry.”

Around that same time, Klaus committed suicide and his father did not attend the funeral. “Suddenly, I knew I had a critical mass for a film,” said Pawlikowski. “There was the historical context that was also psychological. And this triangular family drama.”

It’s also the first time Pawlikowski is dealing with real people, although he fictionalizes freely. He refers to Erika’s homosexuality as an American journalist flirts with her. “It’s hinted that she had a relationship with Betty, one of the journalists who crops up,” said Pawlikowski. “And Betty has certain expectations. Erika just cuts it short now, because she’s on a mission, and that affair is long in the past.” (Erika is also, fascinatingly, married to gay British poet W.H. Auden.)

Pawlikowski, who studied German literature in Germany, said that Mann was gay, “but super repressed,” he said. “He sublimated it in his work. No one thinks he never acted upon it. He was writing about it [‘Death in Venice’], but quite overtly in his diaries about his fantasies. He had crushes and loves for certain men throughout his life. That’s what so annoys Erika at some point. He turns everything into words, he turns everything into art, and he exploits his feelings, repressed passions, and fantasies creatively. He even wrote in one of his early diaries that he desired young Klaus. His diaries were in a safe in Munich in 1933 when they escaped. The big fear was that the Nazis are going to get hold of these diaries. There was a secret mission organized by Erika to rescue the diaries from the Nazis.”

In West Germany, Erika attends a fancy cocktail party, where she runs into a handsome man who turns out to be her ex-husband (Joachim Meyerhoff), a Nazi actor. He tells her she had it easy, with her languages, skills, activities, and rich father. The bile rises in Hüller’s face until she whips out her hand and slaps him. “Everyone assumes she slaps him because he’s a Nazi, but she slaps him because he hit a nerve, because she was a nepo baby,” said Pawlikowski. “Without the father, they would have no money, no contacts, none of this lifestyle that they had. They lived on the Riviera, drove around, were super well-educated, and had fantastic connections.”

Of course Pawlikowski went to Germany’s most lauded actress to play Erika. In the slap scene, “You watch the transformation of her face, and it really, really happens,” said Pawlikowski. “She doesn’t seem to be acting. She has this fake smile, and then in her eyes, what happens there? There was one take where things come to the surface, brilliantly, in a way that’s not scripted and not acted, it mysteriously unfolds.” (Given the recent Academy Award rule changes, Hüller could land two Best Actress slots and a third for Supporting for “Project Hail Mary.” And still to come is “Digger.”)

For the single take prologue, Pawlikowski kept sculpting it with Diehl, taking things out, putting them back in, to reach the right length and cadence. “August was good at that jazzy approach, playing back and forth with you,” he said. “He was totally open to that musical approach to performance. The whole thing had an integrity to it.”

Klaus pops up in the movie a few times like a hovering ghost. “That was a tricky decision,” said Pawlikowski. “I’ve never done that in my life. But this astral projection, if somebody dies, it has been recorded, and [Erika] is so missing and craving him.”

One of Erika Mann’s many skills was driving, which she does in the movie, ferrying Mann around in a giant glossy Buick. “She did long distance rallies,” said Pawlikowski. “And drove often with Klaus. They drove to Kazakhstan, across the Steppes. She wrote with Klaus about driving around the Riviera, and she was behind the wheel. [The Buick] was a difficult car to drive, so Sandra had to really practice a lot, and she’s a really good driver herself. But this car is really heavy, and the gears are tricky, so it took a bit of prep.”

As for the look of the film, cinematographer Łukasz Żal returns, bringing far more camera movement than before. “Everything results from the material, it’s not like I’m imposing this style,” said Pawlikowski. “I like the photography to be strong and concentrated, so that’s the basic principle, but then you do whatever is right. It’s a road movie, but the camera moves when it has to move, but it doesn’t move just to have a bit of cinematic gesture. It’s super primitive and simple, like in silent movies, like the old films. When the camera started to move, it was only to get to get somewhere interesting.”

One spectacular sequence at the start of the film shows Thomas and Erika Mann looking through the car window at the wreckage of the war. “We needed to have an archival moment without using archives,” said Pawlikowski. “We found a street, which was pretty damaged, in a part of Poland which used to belong to Germany. We built some ruins in the foreground, but they’re not painted in, they’re really there. And we found the right extras to look right and busy themselves, and then with digital we painted out satellite dishes and modern windows. We wanted to establish this basic principle where you have an intimate relationship at the center, father-daughter in a capsule, they’re protected from the world. The whole film is about a big vista and a small relationship.”

[Editor’s note: Spoilers for the conclusion of the film follow.]

At the end of the movie, as the Manns leave Weimar to go back West, they see a ruin of an old church. They skip out on their escort and enter the church. “It’s a mutual understanding and urge to see something that’s not official, that’s not part of the official program,” said Pawlikowski. “They’re tuning the organ, which is damaged, when they come in. They happen to play a Bach chorale, play it badly, but still strong enough for us to be moved, and it’s only more moving because it’s a broken organ, and it’s bad. But it still works.”

The music opens up the floodgates for the audience as they mourn Klaus and feel the elegy for everything that’s lost. “You don’t know how to achieve it,” said Pawlikowski. “It’s not so easy, because you write it, imagine it, play the music, and you get moved. But we have to find a church. Then we have to find an organ to put in that church. Then we have to like create an atmosphere where the actors do it in an accidental organic way: how do you engineer that? By the time we shot the scene, they were really close, Sandra and Hanns, and Hanns had some personal grief that he was working through, so the first take, it worked. She takes his hand. That’s the beauty of cinema, when you have good photography and within it you have things that seem to unfold mysteriously rather than like pressing buttons.”

“Fatherland” premiered at the 2026 Cannes Film Festival.

entry.title: ‘The Only Living Pickpocket in New York’ Review: An Old School Thief Holds on in the Age of Apple Pay
entry.summary: John Turturro stars in 'The Only Living Pickpocket in New York.' Read our Sundance review.
entry.content:
[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on January 28, 2026 at the 2026 Sundance Film Festival. Sony Pictures Classics will release the film in theaters on Friday, October 23.]

It’s become commonplace in recent years: movies set in New York, telling distinctly New York stories, yet shot entirely somewhere else like Ireland. Given Hollywood’s economic slowdown, an indie production can be forgiven for doing whatever it takes to get a film made. Still, many films no longer seem interested in even attempting to suspend disbelief about place.

Which makes ”The Only Living Pickpocket in New York” feel like a minor miracle and a welcome update to the New York crime movie genre. Writer/director Noah Segan shoots not only in Manhattan, but across the city’s outer boroughs like the Bronx, Queens, and Brooklyn, capturing a New York that feels authentic rather than postcard-ready. The film’s most satisfying image arrives late: a 360 view of the harbor skyline seen not from lower Manhattan but from the murky New Jersey shoreline, lensed by Sam Levy with bracing clarity. Though the credits list a Los Angeles unit, its scenes disappear seamlessly into the world of the film. 

Related Stories
Daniel Pemberton on Scoring ‘Without a Map,’ from ‘Project Hail Mary’ to David Byrne and Elon Musk
‘Wicker’ Review: Olivia Colman Rides Alexander Skarsgård’s Wood in Bawdy Sex Fantasy About Hysterically Horny Villagers

This Sundance-premiering indie drama stars John Turturro in a controlled, assured performance as Harry Lehman, an old-school pickpocket shaped by decades on New York’s streets. He’s a con man guided by a code. A funk-inflected score — think ”The Payback”-era James Brown — may land a bit heavy-handed, but it effectively establishes a tone of Big Apple toughness that moves into a rhythm measured in city blocks and subway stops.

Segan, a protégé of Rian Johnson whose T-Street banner produced the microbudget film along with MRC, delivers a script that moves with confidence and precision. The visual language toggles purposefully between wide shots and tight close-ups, mirroring Harry’s ability to survey a room and zero in on his take with surgical precision. Before the opening credits, Harry lifts a wallet from a Wall Street guy on the subway — who only notices the loss once he’s seated at a white-tablecloth lunch downtown.

Harry wears the same gray tweed trench coat and polished brown leather oxfords throughout the film. The coat’s hidden inside pocket — a key tool of the trade — becomes a kind of uniform, like that of a janitor or a waitress — neat, understated and designed to disappear. But Turturro doesn’t rely on wardrobe or makeup to sell the character. Harry is a man of few words, so the performance hinges on his physical control and interiority. Turturro delivers both. His pickpocket research is evident — he practiced by lifting from cast and crew — and his movements register with quiet confidence. Harry doesn’t flare up when threatened; he turns inward, calculates, and seizes upon his next move chameleonlike.

Petty theft in Harry’s world follows strict rules: analogue only. No credit cards. No fraud. Just cash and pawnable items destined for resale. When Harry brings his take to Ben, a pawnshop dealer played with steady warmth by Steve Buscemi, he explains that his Wall Street mark carried “all platinum cards” but no cash. The problem is immediately clear: Harry’s expertise hasn’t vanished, but its value has shrunk in a consumer economy dominated by Apple Pay and swipe-lock security.

That friction between analogue and digital fuels one of the film’s central tensions and produces its best humor. In one scene, Harry hands Ben an external data card to load onto Ben’s ancient, 40-pound desktop computer. The machine can’t even read it, yet still manages to alert the card’s owner. “That’s how they get ya,” Harry and Ben mutter, realizing the system demands an upgrade. Later, Harry refers to a corrupted file as having “an illness,” prompting a Gen-Z character to translate: he actually meant virus.

The ensemble cast gives the film its emotional weight. Tatiana Maslany — unrecognizable, as usual — leaves a devastating impression as Harry’s estranged daughter. Harry’s wife Rosie, unable to walk or speak and requiring constant care, is rendered with extraordinary sensitivity. Through the smallest facial shifts and precise physical stillness, the actor conveys a full inner life. A brief but piercing detail completes the portrait: Rosie’s once high-pitched voice, preserved on an answering machine Harry refuses to discard, offers a glimpse of the woman she once was. Lori Tan Chinn charms as a cantankerous Chinatown grandmother, while Jamie Lee Curtis makes a memorable meal of her single scene as a mob boss.

The film’s boldest choice may be what it refuses to show. No guns are waved. No bodies pile up. Violence exists as pressure rather than spectacle. When Harry discovers a gun in one of his hauls, he tosses it into the trash. When Ben’s shop windows are smashed, we find him stunned on the floor, clutching a bat. ”The Only Living Pickpocket in New York” proves that crime stories don’t need bloodshed and gratuitous violence to land with force. 

What emerges is a New York crime drama attuned to the present moment, one that makes space for aging lifers like Harry and Ben alongside younger characters born bluetooth enabled. Everyone struggles to remain in a city where rent keeps climbing and even five-generation families can’t hold onto their homes. The film treats New York itself as a character — not just Manhattan, and certainly not only the Upper East Side — moving with restraint and confidence, grounded in the primary source of its charm: real New Yorkers.

Crucially, the film avoids the trap of scolding younger generations or romanticizing the past. “I like that they don’t just get put on the shelf,” a woman sitting next to me at the Sundance premiere whispered as the credits rolled, phone already back in hand. She’s right. Harry adapts, relying on Ben’s Gen-Z relative (Victoria Moroles), a computer whiz who handles the digital transactions Harry would never be able to —or want to — master.

It’s impossible not to root for Harry and Ben: two flawed, aging men sustained by skills learned the hard way. They pick locks by feel, break into old cars with pennies, trade favors, maintain relationships, and above all, know how to “work,” as Harry puts it, actual human beings. Ultimately ”The Only Living Pickpocket in New York” shows us that old school and new school aren’t opposites. Like the city’s many seeming contradictions, they are meant to coexist.

Grade: A

“The Only Living Pickpocket in New York” premiered at the 2026 Sundance Film Festival.

entry.title: Daniel Pemberton on Scoring ‘Without a Map,’ from ‘Project Hail Mary’ to David Byrne and Elon Musk
entry.summary: 'Project Hail Mary,' 'Musk,' and 'Ink' composer Daniel Pemberton talks to IndieWire's 'Screen Talk' podcast. Interview.
entry.content:
Oscar-nominated composer Daniel Pemberton is a quadruple threat — at least — this year with scores in four movies, as well as the TV series “Slow Horses.”

The British film music writer composed the soundtracks to movies including “The Drama,” with its mischievous flutes recorded at Abbey Road Studios; “Masters of the Universe”; and Oscar contenders “Ink,” “Project Hail Mary,” and “Musk.” On this week’s edition of IndieWire’s “Screen Talk” podcast, co-hosts Anne Thompson and Ryan Lattanzio spoke to Pemberton about his multi-hyphenate journey to composing, which began in video games but included breakout work on Ridley Scott’s “The Counselor.”

Related Stories
‘Wicker’ Review: Olivia Colman Rides Alexander Skarsgård’s Wood in Bawdy Sex Fantasy About Hysterically Horny Villagers
‘The Only Living Pickpocket in New York’ Added a Secret Extra Shoot Day to Break Some Location Rules

“With ‘Hail Mary,’ it was like it had no map, and it was like we gotta make this up as we go along. And that’s thrilling, but also terrifying. And so we spent a huge amount of time, like, just trying out ideas, experimenting, finding unusual textures and sounds, approaches, and that would slowly feed itself into the movie or end up in the bin,” said Pemberton, who also wrote an original song called “Let Me Sell You a Dream” that’s sung by David Byrne in Alex Gibney’s “Musk.” (Gibney was the special guest on last week’s episode of “Screen Talk.”)

Elsewhere on the podcast, we also review (i.e., eviscerate) Taika Waititi’s confoundingly awful dystopian sci-fi movie “Klara and the Sun,” an adaptation of Nobel Prize-winning author Kazuo Ishiguro and starring Jenna Ortega, who’s on a big-screen losing streak after terrible reviews for her last several movies. Like her co-star Amy Adams, she’s faring better these days on television (see Netflix’s “Wednesday”).

We also catch up on “I Play Rocky” and the latest developments in the awards season race — plus, the C-suite freefall happening at Netflix amid the ousting of film head Dan Lin.

Listen to the episode below or on your preferred podcast platform.

entry.title: ‘Wicker’ Review: Olivia Colman Rides Alexander Skarsgård’s Wood in Bawdy Sex Fantasy About Hysterically Horny Villagers
entry.summary: Sundance: Eleanor Wilson and Alex Huston Fischer's bawdy fantasy 'Wicker' stars Olivia Colman, who falls for a man made of wood (Alexander Skarsgard).
entry.content:
[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on January 25, 2026 at the 2026 Sundance Film Festival. Black Bear will release the film in limited theaters on Friday, October 23 with expansion to follow on Friday, October 30.]

A kooky sex-crazed folk tale in search of a larger purpose beyond its whimsical premise, Eleanor Wilson and Alex Huston Fischer’s “Wicker” stars Olivia Colman as a prickly fisherwoman who emerges from the fringes of a seaside village to task a basketmaker (Peter Dinklage) with weaving her a husband. That husband is played by a delightfully deadpan Alexander Skarsgård as a man made entirely of wicker fibers, a face that looks like a woven espadrille stretched over a human skull.

Related Stories
‘The Only Living Pickpocket in New York’ Added a Secret Extra Shoot Day to Break Some Location Rules
Tom Skerritt, ‘Alien’ and ‘M*A*S*H’ Star, Dies at 93

This raunchy period romp arrives in spirit of Geoffrey Chaucer’s for-its-time X-rated “Canterbury Tales” and with an A24-ready, Academy-ratioed crisp visual style serviced by cinematographer Lol Crawley (“The Brutalist”). Sure, the premise — originating from a story called “The Wicker Husband” by Ursula Wills-Jones — is a novel one destined to grab attention. But that gets a bit lost in the cast of characters the filmmakers pack into the story, an ensemble of hysterically horny villagers beset by a seeming spell of sexual frustration, and for whom the arrival of this wicker man, played by Skarsgård, upends all their days and ways, tickling their hearts and loins.

Colman’s fisherwoman is largely derided by the villagers for her inside-and-out smelly disposition and crabby countenance, but she keeps the settlement in foodstuff, bringing slimy fish acquired from the nearby river daily to the townsfolk. “Wicker” is a period film with no specific period to call its own, though you could clock its setting as somewhere in the 1800s. Or 1600s. Whatever; this is not your mother’s olden-times cinematic fable. Those unnamed villagers include a tailor (Nabhaan Rizwan), his miserable tradwife (Elizabeth Debicki, radiantly beautiful and magnetic onscreen), her prudish sister (Marli Siu), a wildly incompetent doctor (Richard E. Grant), and many more.

Wilson and Huston Fischer’s film cuts away from the central action involving Colman and Skarsgård to make space for these other individual stories, even as some get washed away in the sameness of their shared suffering. Flesh wounds, fetid moppets, breastmilk-leaking nipples, and sudden gushes of blood make for a Monty Python-style of ribald humor that will alienate and enchant in equal measure.

“Wicker” is at its most naughtily hilarious, however, in the outrageous lovemaking between Colman and Skarsgård. She’s an embittered spinster long overdue for a roll in the hay (or, in this case, with the hay) who lustily slobs on her new husband’s log. (Such puns are par for the course in a screenplay that even employs “gagging” in its modernly outfitted parlance.) And literally, while it’s kept offscreen, the nifty sound design created by Andy Neil allows us to hear the wicker husband’s, uh, growing tumescence that enables him to vigorously rail his fisherwoman wife into squeams and squirms of overwhelming ecstasy. So much so that a bed is broken, and it’s one he’s, who knew, equipped to fix. Husband material, indeed. The lore of how such a wicker man is created, and whether or not he can conceive, or whether or not his sex might be potentially painful given that it’s literally wrought out of coarse natural fibers, isn’t explained so much as it is not the primary interest of the director/screenwriting pair.

Alexander Skarsgård starring in a period fable as a piece of fuckable furniture might not have been top of mind in terms of what you’re expecting from the actor who has recently done such brilliant work in “Succession,” “Pillion,” and “The Moment.” But even as the tall Swedish actor is tasked with overembellishing given the prostheses he’s bound behind opposite very real human actors, you emerge from “Wicker” with the sense that no other actor could have played this creature, coolly soothing as a presence and an even romantic one, too.

While Colman’s recent stint of playing blowzy, socially alienating women onscreen (from “The Favourite” to “Empire of Light”) is starting to feel like an overcooked trope, she imbues the fisherwoman with grounded pathos that rises above the rest of the movie’s airy whimsy. When a tragic accident strikes late into the film, her emotional collapse feels piercingly real despite the fabulosity surrounding her. Plus, the comic ridiculousness, as repetitive as it may grow, of her sexual rampage with the wicker man feels singularly like something only Colman could sell.

You might wish that “Wicker” had spent more time with the other villagers it weaves into the frames, whether Dinklage’s hovel-dwelling basket wizard, Máté Mészáros’ local drunkard, or Gustav Lindh’s lithe and undersexed bottlewasher. But you have to commend the filmmakers — on their second outing after 2020’s somewhat twee science-fiction outing “Save Yourselves!” — for widening the berth for so many characters in such feature-length time. Crawley’s images, too, elevate what could have been schlocky material (and what of someone like Chaucer or Edmund Spenser, great perverted English writers whom this movie homages, wasn’t working in schlock?) into a quirkfest gilded with prestigious trappings.

At the fibrous heart of the movie, though, is Skarsgård as a taciturn man made of wood whose soul is hardly made of such, and a relationship you root for opposite Colman’s emotionally twisty turn. “Wicker” threatens to feel largely like a logline writ into something grander (i.e., a short story with a wild idea stretched into a feature), but these actors are irresistibly weird and wonderful, as only they could be.

Grade: B

“Wicker” premiered at the 2026 Sundance Film Festival.

entry.title: ‘The Only Living Pickpocket in New York’ Added a Secret Extra Shoot Day to Break Some Location Rules
entry.summary: Writer-director Noah Segan and producers Leopold Hughes and Katie McNeill talk about leaning into New York's energy and working with John Turturro.
entry.content:
As the title promises, writer-director Noah Segan‘s “The Only Living Pickpocket in New York” is a kind of dual character study, a love letter to both its protagonist (played by John Turturro in a career-best performance) and the city in which he lives. It has become a cliché to say that the setting is a character in a movie, but in “The Only Living Pickpocket” it really is — the city lives and breathes and adds texture to the story and depth and definition to the characters in the way that it does in the best films of Martin Scorsese, Spike Lee, and Nicole Holofcener.

Ironically, shooting in the city was the first battle Segan and the producers had to fight. “ It’s called ‘The Only Living Pickpocket in New York,’ and we had this huge debate about rebates and maybe going to Serbia or Bosnia or whatever,” producer Leopold Hughes told IndieWire. “I was really proud that we stuck to our guns on that and made them [shoot in New York].” That said, Hughes, who is British, quickly learned that shooting in New York was a very unique experience.

Related Stories
Tom Skerritt, ‘Alien’ and ‘M*A*S*H’ Star, Dies at 93
Cinema Eye Honors Unveil Nominees for 2027’s Best Documentary Films and Series

“I’d never shot in New York before,” Hughes said. “We were a Tier One movie [referring to the IATSE union tiers for low-budget, independent films], and I have never had a video village just in a live road where there are trucks, and then a guy comes up saying, ‘I’m gonna shoot everybody.’ And I’m like, Okay, should we do something about this?’ And everyone’s like, ‘Don’t worry about that guy.’ Weirdly, it was a very freeing experience, because in England, there is no way we would’ve ever been able to do this.”

According to producer Katie McNeill, the key to shooting in New York is finding like-minded individuals, both in terms of cast and crew, who understand what it takes to get a movie made. “Like, instead of spending money on trailers that are going to be so far from where we’re shooting that you’re going to spend no time in them, let’s get a little scrappier and find ways to put more of that money on the screen,” McNeill said. “The secret to working in New York at this budget level is working with casts that are like, ‘I’m okay. I’m buying into the idea that I don’t need a fancy trailer.”

Segan and his producers credited executive producer Johnny Holland with setting the tone. “It’s a very New York tone, where we really went for forgiveness over permission,” Segan said. “ Even to the degree of saying to people, ‘Listen, thank you for agreeing to act in this movie. You don’t have a trailer.’ That’s the cost of doing a movie like this, and it’s the fun of doing a movie like this.” The director added that it’s not enough to merely have a “no jerks” policy to get the job done in New York — you have to have a “we are having a great time” policy.

“Like, what will make this fun?” Segan said. “And when you have a problem, how do you solve it by laughing? How do you solve it with positivity? You just want to create an environment where people want to show up for work the next day. And everybody needs something different. Once you’re in production, the job is about, what do people need every day? You get sort of granular and ask, what does this person need? What does that person need? And you just start running around as a unit to try to accomplish that.”

Although “The Only Living Pickpocket in New York” technically had a 25-day shooting schedule, the producers added a 26th day that yielded many of the film‘s most quintessentially New York images. “We knew there were certain shots  we wanted to get that were going to add a lot of scale to the film,” McNeill said. “But if we tried to get them early in our shoot, we would run into the possibility that If we got in trouble, all of our permits would be pulled, and we wouldn’t be able to do the other work that we needed.”

The filmmakers therefore decided that if they were going to break any rules, they would break them all on the last day — a plan that required cooperation from Turturro, who was more than game. “You have a contract with an actor a certain period of time,” McNeill said. “But as we were getting closer and closer to the end of the schedule, John said, ‘If you need more from me I’m here. Whatever you need.’ And we were like, ‘Let’s just spend a day running around the New York subway system.'”

“One time two cops got on the subway when we were shooting with no permit,” Segan said. “It’s not even like we couldn’t afford it, you can’t get a permit to shoot on a subway. You just have to do it and pray and hope.” When the cops got on the train and saw Turturro there with the crew, Segan and McNeill looked at each other worriedly, figuring they had pushed their luck too far. “They walk toward us, and the train stops, and they get out and they leave. As the doors are closing, one turns to the other and says, ‘Yeah, I told you it was him.'”

The key, according to McNeill, was keeping a small footprint. “We had maybe 10 people working that day,” she said. “There are certain things that you can only capture if you don’t have a giant production machine. Luckily, John couldn’t have been happier to make a film this way — it was probably the most exhilarating day he ever had on a film set because he was getting away with something.” The producers also discovered that Turturro’s status as a beloved New York actor went a long way when it came to getting the local authorities on board with stealing shots.

“There’s a shot where he comes out of the police station, and we weren’t allowed to go in there,” Hughes said. “John just walked in and said, ‘Hey guys, we’re gonna shoot something. We’re gonna come in and out.’ And the cops were like, ‘Oh yeah, get in here. Sign the book.’ There were so many times where I thought, there’s no way they’re going to let us do this, and they just said, ‘Great, yeah, do whatever you want.’ That’s the beauty of John.”

A Sony Pictures Classics release, “The Only Living Pickpocket in New York” is currently playing in theaters.

entry.title: Tom Skerritt, ‘Alien’ and ‘M*A*S*H’ Star, Dies at 93
entry.summary: Tom Skerritt, whose acting career spanned seven decades and played Dallas in "Alien" and Duke in "M*A*S*H," has died. He was 93.
entry.content:
Tom Skerritt, the American screen actor who was first billed in Ridley Scott’s horror classic “Alien” (1979) and sustained a career spanning more than seven decades, died Wednesday of natural causes, according to media reports. He was 93.

Skerritt first rose to prominence with a breakout turn in Robert Altman’s Korean War comedy “M*A*S*H,” playing the surgeon Duke Forrest. He was third-billed in the feature, after then-more-established stars Donald Sutherland and Elliott Gould. The role launched him to a prolific Hollywood career that saw him garner more than 100 screen credits. He kept acting through the final years of his life, with his most recent project being a supporting role in the 2025 Western “Broke” starring Wyatt Russell.

More to come…

entry.title: Cinema Eye Honors Unveil Nominees for 2027’s Best Documentary Films and Series
entry.summary: 2027 Cinema Eye Honors reveal its Audience Choice Prize Longlist, its Unforgettables Honorees, its Broadcast nominees, and its Shorts List.
entry.content:
The Cinema Eye Honors, one of the main bellwethers for the Best Documentary Feature race, began its 20th annual celebrations with a first wave of awards announcements for its 2027 ceremony.

17 films made it onto its Audience Choice Prize Longlist, including Sundance breakouts like “American Doctor” and “Once Upon a Time in Harlem” as well as recent box office successes “The History of Concrete” and “You Can See Everything.”

The organization’s Unforgettable Honorees, an award celebrating on-camera collaborators, were also announced with the 2027 winners coming from six films: Dr. Thaer Ahmad, Dr. Mark Perlmutter and Dr. Feroze Sidhwa from “American Doctor,” E. Jean Carroll from “Ask E. Jean,” Soraya Akhlaghi from “A Fox Under a Pink Moon,” Billie Jean King from “Give Me the Ball,” Israa from “One in a Million,” and Amy Goodman from “Steal This Story, Please!”

Related Stories
‘Moonlight’ Turns 10: Tarell Alvin McCraney on the Film’s Lasting Legacy and That Best Picture Mix-Up
Artists Equity’s Amy Baer on Building a Sustainable Indie Model with Movies That Don’t Star Matt Damon or Ben Affleck

On the Broadcast side, nominees were announced for five different categories, from Outstanding Achievement in Broadcast Film to Outstanding Achievement in Broadcast Editing. The annual Shorts List, spotlighting 10 of the year’s top documentary short films, including “They’re Here” co-directed by Oscar winner Laura Poitras, was also part of the announcement.

Finally, “Hoop Dreams,” Steve James’ documentary masterpiece, will receive the Legacy Award, which is presented to a classic nonfiction film that continues to inspire today’s working filmmakers. James will accept the award on behalf of his team members Peter Gilbert (Producer and DP), Frederick Marx (Producer and Editor), Adam Singer (Sound Recordist), Gordon Quinn (Executive Producer and founder of Kartemquin Films), Bill Haugse (Editor), Marcie McCall (Kartemquin) and Ben Sidran (Composer).

Cinema Eye will celebrate its 20th annual Awards Ceremony on Monday, January 11, 2027.

entry.title: ‘Moonlight’ Turns 10: Tarell Alvin McCraney on the Film’s Lasting Legacy and That Best Picture Mix-Up
entry.summary: Oscar-winning screenwriter Tarell Alvin McCraney reflects on the beginnings of 'Moonlight,' to he and director Barry Jenkins winning an Academy Award.
entry.content:
The word playwright and screenwriter Tarell Alvin McCraney uses to describe his thoughts on the journey his deeply personal film “Moonlight” continues to have is “incredible.” Wednesday, October 21, marks 10 years since the Best Picture Oscar winner was released to the masses. ”Seeing it now is worth the price of admission,” said the Best Adapted Screenplay Oscar winner to IndieWire over Zoom.

An adaptation of his unproduced play “In Moonlight Black Boys Look Blue,” written with director Barry Jenkins, “Moonlight” still has McCraney asking himself the fundamental question, “‘Who am I and who can I be?’ And that’s powerful.”

Related Stories
Artists Equity’s Amy Baer on Building a Sustainable Indie Model with Movies That Don’t Star Matt Damon or Ben Affleck
Don’t Get the Wrong Idea About ‘The Dropout’

The current Geffen Playhouse artistic director, who is still working on many TV and film projects he is not yet allowed to discuss, said, “I’m still expanding like the universe. And the moment that I stop, the moment that I just sit in it, then where am I?”

Read on for more of McCraney reflecting on “Moonlight” at 10 below.

How “Moonlight” Came to Be

“So ‘In Moonlight Black Boys Look Blue’ was a film, a screenplay that I wrote in 2003, right after the death of my mother. She died of AIDS-related complications. And I had written a play called ‘The Brothers Size’ for my entry into the Yale School of Drama and the script called ‘In Moonlight Black Boys Look Blue.’ I had written both of them because, one, I was making an application for grad school, but two, my teacher, Rafael Lima, who was our playwriting and screenplay teacher in high school, always told me that if a story was coming to you visually, then it’s a film. If you heard it, it was a play. So ‘In Moonlight Black Boys Look Blue’ was always slated to be a film because it was coming to me in images, but I’d written it in a kind of hybrid, what I call a medium length.

“It wasn’t a full feature at the time. I previously had written a short in high school called ‘Silent Type,’ and it was more about me trying to put down the memories I was having of growing up in Liberty City. Now, I understand it’s something most people do when losing a parent. They sort of start trying to recollect their earliest memories and put them back together again. So that’s how ‘In Moonlight Black Boys Look Blue’ came about. But in 2003, an indie film about a gay kid in Miami was probably a hard feat, especially for a just-recently-graduated undergrad. So André Holland, who I met later, had read a copy of it, Glenn Davis, who runs Steppenwolf, we had all read a copy and tried to make it into a film in Chicago. Then I quickly sort of said, ‘No, this is where we stay.’ And it stayed in my computer for probably another 10 years until I met Barry Jenkins in around 2012, 2013.

“We were both making a film in a film festival here in Miami. We had a couple meetings, and found out we grew up blocks away from each other. Barry said, ‘Look, I want to make this into a film. I’ve read the script.’ Our friend Andrew Hevia had given it to him. He said, ‘I think I can make this into a full feature.’ I was like, ‘Great, we should.’ He didn’t believe me a few times. This is before there was an A24 or Plan B involved. So I think he thought I didn’t believe him. He kept going back, getting more support, and saying, ‘Look, we’re going to make this into a film.’ I kept going, ‘Yes, yes you are.’

“So even to this day, he said, ‘Yeah, you did have to say yes to me a few times before I believed you.’ But yeah, that’s how we came together on the film. Barry did an incredible job of turning it into a full feature, taking the story that was already there and taking it from a place of memory into a place of palpability and something that we all could feel.”

On the Role YoungArts Played in “Moonlight” Being Made

“I have had an incredible education in art thanks to Miami. Miami’s art has been nurtured in a real way by YoungArts and The National Foundation for the Advancement of the Arts, specifically young artists, because it brings in artists from all over the world.

“I remember sneaking out of playwriting class to go to YoungArts to see the YoungArts finalists and thinking, ‘Those dancers are doing what I’m supposed to be doing in their form right now. Their dedication, their ability to control their body and use their technique is — ’ And I’m just over here in this acting class trying to remember my lines. I just thought even then, ‘I’ve got to get my shit together.’

“And so YoungArts has really paved a way for that. They have really dedicated themselves to nurturing the local artists, but also bringing in young artists and supporting them for longer stretches of time. That’s been so helpful. Andrew Hevia, who was an arts finalist, is the reason why Barry Jenkins and I met each other because he was producing films and said to us, ‘Hey, you both are Miami. You both have Miami connections. You should know each other.’

“YoungArts was instrumental in giving us space to do pre-production for ‘Moonlight.’ That organization has really carved a path for arts in this community in a way that national foundations rarely do. So I’m ever grateful for them and wish them nothing but success and hope that other national organizations, that the government, that our local folks really help celebrate them and keep them around for a long time.”

On How He Saw “Moonlight” for the First Time

“Watching it for the first time, even in New York, because though I was near and helping on production, I was not on set. There were just too many places that they were going to that were places I had grown up and places that I had actually lived in. So I didn’t know how I would feel sitting on a set in those moments. But I do remember watching a great deal of those moments on film, in screening rooms, and it was beautiful. First I thought, ‘Wow, I’m so glad that this exists. I’m so glad that these memories have been immortalized in these ways with these incredible artists rendering it for all of us to see.’

“Seeing it at TIFF, something else happened, which was like, ‘Oh, wow. And now I’m sharing all of these things with 2,200 people.’ And I did not expect that. I will tell you, and I’ve said to many people, whether people think it’s naïve or shortsighted, I really thought, ‘Yeah, a few hundred thousand people may see this film in total.’ I grew up on indie films. I grew up in Miami going to places like O Cinema, and my mentor would take us to art films all the time here in the cinema. So it was something that we were used to even when the blockbusters like ‘Bad Boys’ were being made here, we were still watching ‘Before Night Falls.’

“So I was used to that and thought, ‘This is going to be a great addition to that.’ It blew my mind to see that it was going beyond that, that it was pushing past that, that this was going to be seen by maybe millions of people. I don’t know that I’ve still come to full terms with that. It’s the reason why I look shocked and surprised when people want to talk to me about the film even now.”

On Mahershala Ali’s Oscar-Winning Performance as Juan in “Moonlight”

“Mahershala and I crossed paths prior to ‘Moonlight’ because he was supposed to be in my play ‘In the Red and Brown Water.’ He is an incredible actor and was on stage then, and we were trying to get him into this play, and he sent me this note saying he’s so sorry he had to go do this other play and we couldn’t do it. So we ended up not working together on that, but I admired his work and loved seeing him on stage and on television as well. At the time, he was filming two or three shows.

“So when it came to the moment where Barry said, ‘Hey, here’s who we’re going to for Juan,’ I said, ‘Yeah, that’ll do.’ I always felt like it made sense, and the character clearly is based on someone who made a deep influence on my life as a young person. So there was no doubt in my mind that Mahershala would be extraordinary.”

On Naomie Harris’ Oscar-Nominated Performance as Paula in “Moonlight”

“It was incredible. She had about three or four days on set to film all of that. I didn’t know Naomie before, but she is an incredible artist who came in and just went, and it was extraordinary to watch. Sometimes it was hard to watch because she just went to this place where — that character couldn’t be more not like her. And especially in the earlier moments where she really embodies a lot of what my mother stood for, and then in the decline that she has in the film, some of the terror that my mother was going through. Thankfully, Barry kept the reconciliation that happens in the film that was in the script. He kept that and actually built on it in a way that was really gorgeous and really beautiful. So I was ever grateful for her portrayal, for going there, because she could have played it safe and she didn’t.”

On the Visual Legacy of “Moonlight”

“At the time, when we were both making and premiering the film, the democratizing, or the ability for folks to make film or visual depictions has exploded. In fact, the next film that I did make was shot on an iPhone. So the ability for people to make visual depictions and reach towards cinematic success became more palpable or more accessible. There were a lot of folks who were going, ‘Well, if those folks can do that, I can do this.’ And that was really extraordinary. I had tons of people write and say, ‘This made me go to film school. This made me take up cinematography in a way. This made me become a photographer.’ Literally, I have so many friends who just went, ‘Yeah, I write, but now I’m also a photographer, and I take it seriously, and I’m really about visual lenses.’ So that’s been extraordinary.

“That impact, a lot of it for me was being able to say, ‘Hey, I needed to make this film because I needed to see myself, or at least parts of myself that I wasn’t seeing.’ And I think a lot of folks went, ‘Yeah, I need to do the same.’ And I am grateful for that. And that happens: Films come along and do that. Films come along, or songs come along, or something happens in art where people go, ‘Oh, that artist really needed to see that depiction of themselves. I feel that, too, and want to do the same.’ So again, it was a gift to me that it is happening for other folks.

“When you think of a depiction of Black folk, specifically Black queer folks, there is a level of intimacy that the film has that folks recognized as ‘Oh wow, you can get that vulnerable on a subject that isn’t often seen.’ And again, when I say vulnerable, I mean the closeness of the shots, the deep peering into eyes that we hadn’t seen before. We’ve done that on tons of film. If you go back and look at some of the noir, you can get tons of close-ups of X, Y, and Z, but you watch things like ‘Ordinary People,’ and you see just how close and intimate, into the heat, that the camera gets. There are, of course, examples of those rituals like the baptism that happens to Chiron/Little by Juan, but they’re fewer and far between. The film is saying, ‘Hey, you can get closer to this and do more of it.’ And there’s a lot of filmmakers who have found their ideology, their way in through that, and found their own unique stamp to put on it, which is extraordinary.”

On “Moonlight” Entering the Best Adapted Screenplay Category — Even Though the Play Was Never Produced

“‘Fences’ is a play and then was adapted into a film, and so Adapted made sense. Again, you take a short, and you turn it into a feature length, and that’s an adaptation too. So it felt right to be there, for sure. Barry did really make it into a feature.

“The original script told this story in a very circular way, meaning you woke up and you realized that you would see the day going on of Little, Chiron, and Black all at once. So you would see one wake up, wash their face, the other get up, wash their face. At some point you realized that this was one life that you were watching. Barry thought, ‘No, we can chapter this out and make this more linear.’

“And then, he, of course, blew up that last 20 to 30 minutes of the film. [It] is an incredible Barry Jenkins lean-in, but peppering tons of shit that I do in my own life. I was like, ‘How did you…’ So yeah, adaptation, absolutely. It was incredible to collaborate with him on that, and I wish we could do it more.”

On Whether “Moonlight” Is Too Enmeshed with the Best Picture Mix-Up with “La La Land”

“It’s one of those things that just is. It’s like in the story, Juan disappears out of Little’s life, and it is just one of those things that is.

“And I don’t think that has tarnished the film in any way. The film is still the film. But yeah, it happened, and I’m grateful for however it manifested. I can’t undo it.

“I remember saying this to my friend Jeremy Pope — not just talking about this, but just life in general — I said, ‘Jay, if you don’t count it all joy, then you won’t stop counting.’ You have to count it all as joy. Every time you have to count it all joy, and it feels like one of those counts. You just count it all joy that we are headed towards this direction, that we’re 10 years out, and that this film that a lot of wonderful people put a lot of incredible work into was recognized in many ways.”

entry.title: ‘The Hunger Games’ Producer Nina Jacobson Talks Using AI to Test ADR Lines Before Recording with Actors: ‘We Would Never Use It’ in the Film
entry.summary: "Hunger Games" franchise producer Nina Jacobson explains AI's place in the post-production process and why the series resonates in Trump's America.
entry.content:
AI is continuing to be implemented in the post-production stages of studio films, though “Hunger Games” franchise producer Nina Jacobson still views it as a “tool for artists” and “not a substitute” for them.

During a conversation with IndieWire editor-in-chief Brent Lang at IndieWire’s Future of Filmmaking Summit in Los Angeles Jacobson said the team used AI approximations of actors to test out new line readings for the upcoming prequel “Sunrise on the Reaping.” Those lines would then be recorded with the cast in traditional automated dialogue replacement process.

“We just finished [post-production], fairly recently, on ‘Sunrise on the Reaping.’ We used [AI] very specifically as a tool — within production, within post-production — while, at the same time, never using it to ever replace any of our artists or anything you see onscreen,” Jacobson said. “When you have ADR you want try out, you used to either have the editor getting in there with the lines you wanted … Just for something you’re trying out that you might not even keep. [AI] is a great tool to use ADR.”

Related Stories
Gen Z Feels ‘Doomed’ Watching AI, but Gen Alpha Feels Differently
WGA East Moves to Block AI Models from Training on Members’ Work with New Software Partner Cloak: ‘Give Agency Back to Writers’

Jacobson went on to explain how the technology has relatively limited applications for her, none of which find their way onto the screen.

“They can duplicate a voice. You can have the thing that you want to go get, or do a slug that actually looks like what you want … But we would still never use it because it’s not our actors,” she continued. “We’d go to our writer for the dialogue. I don’t ask Claude, ‘What should they say?’ I don’t ask Claude to finish the movie for us. But as a tool within production [and] within post-production that advances your work, and ultimately gets you to a better creative outcome, it’s crazy not to make use of the tool that the entire world now seems to be hinging upon.”

The prequel “Sunrise on the Reaping,” in theaters from Lionsgate on November 20, is the sixth film adaptation of Suzanne Collins’ popular young adult books series. The movie franchise first launched in 2012, with three additional entries produced quickly in the immediate years. Lionsgate revived the property in 2023 with the prequel “The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes,” exploring the early politicking of the dystopian world of Panem and how the tyrant President Snow came to power.

“We don’t make the movies unless [Collins] writes a book. We’re not trying to just milk this title,” Jacobson said when asked about the franchise’s longevity. “They speak so much to the way that we live now and how we are living. The last one was really about the allure of authoritarianism. Why do we embrace it as a political system? Why are people drawn to it? … This one is about resistance: the cost of [it, and] the fact that just because something is a certain way today does not mean it always will be. You cannot predict the future based on the status quo.”

“Young people are growing up at a time where it seems impossible that we would ever be able to address climate change or the recession in democracy that we’ve seen across the globe, and yet it is that propaganda that kind of keeps you in that place of believing there’s nothing I can do to make a difference,” Jacobson continued. “Sometimes you won’t see the consequences of your resistance [in] four years, or maybe even in your lifetime. But it still adds up. … Whether you’ve seen none of the movies or all of them, it feels very much like a movie about the times we live in.”

Along with Jacobson’s “Hunger Games” talk, the producer touched on other projects from her film production company Color Force, including the coming “Dirty Dancing” sequel starring Jennifer Grey and HBO’s “Crazy Rich Asians” series. IndieWire’s Future of Filmmaking Summit also included a keynote by directors Phil Lord and Chris Miller, diving into the production of their sci-fi blockbuster “Project Hail Mary,” and a one-on-one with Bill Hader on what he learned making his upcoming feature debut “They Know.”

Watch the complete conversation with Jacobson in the video above.

IndieWire Future of Filmmaking 2026 Summit is presented by AT&T Untold Stories, an impactful multi-year collaboration between AT&T and Tribeca Festival that awards $1.2 million dollars, mentorship, and comprehensive support to the next generation of filmmakers looking to bring their films to the big screen.
